sources.relevance: A crisp rule for disp's erasers: an agent may vanish only once all its ports are free, so erasure is a series of reversible detach steps ending at one isolated leaf, the one place Landauer heat is paid. Any rule that merges wires without a record is SqPO-like and loses information.

sources.title: Space-time reversible graph rewriting (Arrighi, Costes, Maignan 2025)
sources.quote: reversibility forces us to allow for the merger of two node names as the correct inverse operation of node splitting
sources.mechanism: Directed acyclic labelled port graphs rewritten asynchronously at nondeterministically chosen places, in the space-time deterministic framework. Reversibility is redefined so that 'any two closeby snapshots ... must mutually determine each other' (p.1, p.18). Locally-causal evolution cannot pick fresh names globally, so names are built locally: splitting x gives x.l and x.r, merging obeys x.l ∨ x.r = x, and x and x.l cannot coexist. Three characterizations of reversibility are given (formal, axiomatic, constructive); the constructive one is a rewrite system causal in both directions, with sufficient local conditions on rules. Example: time dilation in the spirit of general relativity.
sources.relevance: Matches disp's substrate of random local moves that should be physically reversible. A duplicator copying x leaves x.l and x.r carrying their ancestry, and un-copy is the merge, so no global id table is needed; the reversibility notion tolerates an asynchronous schedule.

key_ideas: There are three places to keep 'where did I come from' while reading shared code, each with its own cost. (a) In the code itself (the removed iso.rs walker parked its context in the tree): one reader per copy of the code. (b) On the token (Danos–Regnier IAM stacks, https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/16874549/Reversible_irreversible_and_optimal_machines.pdf#page=4; Abramsky's address term, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=18): any number of parallel readers of one copy, but tokens of unbounded size. (c) At the sharing point (Geometry of Synthesis's 1-bit set-reset register, https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/Compiling-Affine-Recursion-into-Static-Hardware.pdf#page=6): bounded tokens, but readers take turns at each shared node.

Copying by splitting a tag instead of duplicating: S's copy of z becomes 'two askers, one z, with l/r recorded in the question' (Abramsky's W rules l(l(p(x,y)))<->r(l(p(l(x),y))), https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=18). Rules are partial involutions (each undoes itself), so this is reversible and the tag is the only history; it is undone on the answer's return trip.

Dropping an argument by never asking for it: Abramsky's K is l(x)<->r(r(x)) and 'the second argument ... does not get accessed' (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=14). In a demand-driven core, K and triage's untaken arms are never visited instead of being erased; reclaiming them, and paying heat for it, would be a separate choice (an inference, not from the source).

A mux agent as the cheap alternative to the Dn duplicator: Geometry of Synthesis's diagonal routes a request, remembers which side asked in one bit, and routes the answer back. Energy could then pick between mux (no fuel, one reader at a time) and copy (fuel, parallel), a run-time version of GoS's compile-time choice of whether a circuit 'must be reinstantiated or can be reused' (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2011/09/Compiling-Affine-Recursion-into-Static-Hardware.pdf#page=2).

A reuse/copy dial rather than a fixed choice: the DGoIM's interleaving (passes-only = re-walk, rewrites-first = copy and cache; https://arxiv.org/pdf/1803.00427#page=3) and the PaJAM's backtracking depth k (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.27062#page=5) both slide between cheap-space/slow-time reuse and fast-time/more-space memory. Pure re-walking can be exponentially slow (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.12988#page=2). Every finite k is polynomial, but the degree grows with k (O(n^(6k+5))).

History wires instead of jumps: the JAM's jump ('losing locality and reversibility', https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.27062#page=2) follows a non-local pointer saved in the token's log. On a strand lattice the same shortcut could be a physical strand the token leaves behind and retracts on return, possibly keeping the speedup while staying local and undoable. This is an open design, not a published result.

In a reuse machine, parallelism means many tokens on one shared code plus local join nodes: sync links let tokens cross only when every in-edge is saturated, and the correctness criterion (no switching cycles) gives deadlock freedom (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.3427#page=14). The source covers only the multiplicative fragment, with no sharing by contraction, and does not claim joins are reversible.

One local rule that composes edges can run a whole evaluator in parallel. Virtual reduction composes two adjacent edges into new ones without consuming the originals, which are marked with filters (https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0407055#page=4). PELCR's half-combustion strategy and its garbage collection reach up to 70/80% of ideal speedup. Note that the practical version garbage-collects dead nodes rather than keeping every record.

Name splitting and merging as local provenance: a split node x becomes x.l and x.r, and x.l ∨ x.r = x undoes it (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.03296#page=3). Copies carry their ancestry, so undoing a copy needs no global id table, and reversibility is defined so that it tolerates an asynchronous, nondeterministic schedule.

DPO's no-dangling rule as the erasure discipline (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2204.07175#page=4): a node may be deleted only when no edges outside the match still touch it, which keeps every step reversible. Erasure then becomes reversible detach steps until one isolated leaf. Rules that delete with dangling edges or merge nodes without a record (SqPO, sesqui-pushout) lose information. This is clean for linear rules only.

Landauer trace for tree calculus as a rewrite system (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.02804#page=8): a step records its rule label plus the bindings of the variables it erases. That means z for K, nothing for S, and the untaken arms for triage. Position-free traces and returning the trace as a value need the rules flattened into pure-constructor form first. With sharing by name, a call-by-value machine needs only O(1) history per step (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.09179#page=1).

Sharing levels and bracket operators keep sharing and unsharing correctly matched in Lamping-style graphs. Their cost is the open problem: only conjectured polynomial, and exponential if handled carelessly. Code typable in elementary linear logic needs no brackets at all (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.04240#page=5), a possible typing condition (stratified code) for disp that would keep optimal sharing simple.

field: Universality under reversibility and the tree calculus: what a reversible tree calculus has to keep, where injectivity runs out, and the smallest reversible primitive set that still runs disp (with a trace when needed)

sources.title: Reflective Programs in Tree Calculus (Barry Jay, 2021)
sources.quote: Note that (K) deletes the third argument, (S) duplicates the third argument
sources.mechanism: One operator △. Values are leaf △, stem △x and fork △xy. The building rules only add structure. The book's reduction rules (p.40) are △△yz = y (K), △(△x)yz = yz(xz) (S) and △(△wx)yz = zwx (F). The book itself says K deletes the third argument, S duplicates it, and F 'decomposes the first argument to expose its branches'. Triage appears in the book only as a derived program (sec. 5.7, p.72). The triage-as-a-rule form that disp uses is not in this book. Information is lost in K (drops z) and in F (drops y). S copies z, and undoing that copy needs an equality check. Size and equality are programs within the calculus (p.5, sec. 5.3), and reduction is confluent (sec. 7.5, pp.96-97). Ch.10 (SF-calculus): 'reduction of F does not allow for duplication of any kind' ([p.126](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/barry-jay-personal/tree-calculus/master/tree_book.pdf#page=126)), so copying goes to S. No account of history, garbage or cost.
sources.relevance: Fixes the list of losses a reversible replacement must handle: K's z, the arm F/triage drops and the choice it made, and the inverse of S's copy. Since equality is a tree program, un-copy can be written inside the calculus. SF is a precedent for keeping copying in its own operator.

sources.title: Logical Reversibility of Computation (Charles H. Bennett, 1973)
sources.quote: the history tape is not random
sources.mechanism: A Turing machine written as quadruples: each read-write step and each shift step is a one-to-one map on the whole machine state. Three tapes. Stage 1 runs the program and writes 'the index m as each transition pair is executed' onto the history tape (p.5). Stage 2 copies the output onto a blank tape with history recording suspended. Stage 3 retraces stage 1, which erases the history. What remains is the input plus the output. For one-to-one functions, stages 4-7 swap input and output, then build a history of the inverse computation (stage five) and use it to erase the input. A v-step run needs v history records. The paper also says storage 'can be cut down by breaking the job into a sequence of n segments, each one of which would be performed and retraced' (pp.5-6).
sources.relevance: The standard compute, copy, uncompute recipe. A history entry is a transition index only because each Turing-machine rule overwrites a finite symbol fixed by the rule. Tree calculus's K drops an unbounded subtree, so 'which rule fired' is not enough there; the record must also hold the dropped data (as Di Pierro et al. and Nishida et al. do). For bijective functions, the inverse's history is what erases the input.

sources.title: Time/Space Trade-Offs for Reversible Computation (Charles H. Bennett, 1989)
sources.quote: In reversible pebbling, both the addition and the removal of a pebble require that the predecessors have pebbles
sources.mechanism: Break the run into segments with checkpoints, then do and undo them hierarchically (Table 2). This gives time O(T^(1+ε)) and space O(S log T), or linear time and space O(ST) (abstract, Theorem 1). Checkpoint creation and removal is reversible pebbling of a line graph: a pebble may be added or removed only while its predecessor is pebbled. Theorem 2 and Table 3 ([p.7](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~sbuss/CourseWeb/Math268_2013W/Bennett_Tradeoffs.pdf#page=7)) cover the input-erasing computation of a one-to-one f, built from irreversible algorithms for f and f⁻¹. Each builds a temporary bridge (history or checkpoints) from x to f(x).
sources.relevance: Prices history space against time. The pebble rule is a local condition. A lattice move could check it. But Lange-McKenzie-Tapp note that simulations obeying Bennett's pebble rules need the extra log T factor (p.2), so a local pebble rule alone cannot do better than S log T.

sources.title: Reversible Space Equals Deterministic Space (Lange, McKenzie, Tapp, 2000)
sources.quote: irreversibility of M translates precisely into the fact that Gw is a tree and not simply a line
sources.mechanism: Take the graph of all configurations reachable on input w. Each configuration has one successor, so the graph is a tree. Branching (several predecessors) is exactly where information is lost. The reversible machine runs an Euler tour of this tree with each edge doubled. It alternates two permutations on edge ends: a swap, and a rotation through a locally fixed order of the edge ends at each configuration. The rotation cycles through 'the ordered sequence of all possible predecessors' of a configuration, read off the transition table (pp.7-10). Space stays S(n). Time is exponential in S. No history is stored.
sources.relevance: Names what an irreversible step destroys (which predecessor) and is the space-optimal end of the history spectrum. It needs a finite, locally listable set of predecessors, which a Turing machine has. Under tree-calculus K, any z could have been dropped, so the walk does not apply directly.

sources.title: What Do Reversible Programs Compute? (Axelsen, Glück, 2011)
sources.quote: can compute exactly all injective, computable functions
sources.mechanism: From the abstract, which is all that was fetched: reversible Turing machines compute exactly the injective computable functions. They are 'not strictly classically universal' but support 'RTM-universality'. They are powerful enough to include a self-interpreter. The authors propose r-Turing completeness as the 'gold standard' for reversible languages. The precise definition of RTM-universality (a universal machine mapping (p, x) to (p, [[p]](x))) and the treatment of Landauer embeddings are in the full paper, which could not be fetched (Springer blocked; no open copy found).
sources.relevance: Draws the line: with no trace, a reversible core runs exactly the injective programs. The 'keep the program: (f, x) → (f, f x)' design rests on the full paper's definition of RTM-universality, which was not checked here.

sources.title: A Simple Universal Logic Element and Cellular Automata for Reversible Computing (Kenichi Morita, 2001)
sources.quote: it makes a right turn, and rotates the bar by 90 degrees counterclockwise
sources.mechanism: The rotary element (RE) is a reversible sequential machine with a two-state 'bar', four inputs and four outputs, and a one-to-one move function δ: Q×Σ→Q×Γ. A particle arriving parallel to the bar goes straight. A particle arriving across the bar turns right and rotates the bar. It is bit-conserving: a particle is neither created nor destroyed (p.3). Any reversible Turing machine can be built from REs alone, and 'there is no need to supply a clock signal' (p.2). An RE can be embedded in the 2D reversible cellular automaton P3. P4, cited from earlier work, is a related automaton that embeds reversible two-counter machines. Morita's survey: 'any reversible Turing machine and reversible sequential machine can be built very simply only from REs as a completely garbageless circuit' ([survey p.7](https://web.archive.org/web/20240810230942id_/https://ir.lib.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/25576/files/16460#page=7)). It also cites a 17-state, 5-symbol universal reversible Turing machine ([p.23](https://web.archive.org/web/20240810230942id_/https://ir.lib.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/25576/files/16460#page=23)).
sources.relevance: A physical picture of a conserved particle moving through 1-bit matter: garbage-free, clock-free, embeddable in a lattice, and sequential. It is universal only for injective functions unless given a Landauer embedding.

sources.title: A Structural Approach to Reversible Computation (Samson Abramsky, 2005)
sources.quote: provides the ultimate reversible simulation of the irreversible phenomena of computation
sources.mechanism: Pattern-matching automata with rules (q, r) → (s, q′). The pattern must match the whole term. Rules are left-linear (no variable twice in r), and biorthogonal means both the automaton and its reverse (rules flipped) are orthogonal. Such automata are reversible step by step and 'linear in the sense that... the same variables occur in r and in s' (p.6). Signature: ε, l, r and binary p, reducible to 'one binary operation and one constant—i.e. the pure theory of binary trees' ([p.22](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=22)). Linear application LApp(f,g) = f_rr ∪ f_rl;g;(f_ll;g)*;f_lr is a feedback loop in which l/r tags route the token between function and argument (p.11). Replication !f = {(p(t,u), p(t,v)) | (u,v) ∈ f}, so the copy index rides in the token. Theorem 5.1 gives an affine combinatory algebra with B, C, K, D, δ, F, W (I is definable as C·K·K). Automaton size is linear in term size (p.1). Termination is Σ01-complete (Theorem 8.1, p.25). The boundary: adding boolean constants with a conditional and δ-rules loses biorthogonality. The multiplicative-exponential fragment of linear logic is reversible, but 'this fails for the additives' ([p.25](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=25)), where partial injectivity is lost. On parallelism, Dal Lago et al.: answering requires 'multiple calls to the IAM [interaction abstract machine], which however can proceed in parallel, without any need for synchronization' ([arXiv 1405.3427 p.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1405.3427#page=1)). Danos and Regnier: the reversible interaction machine 'needs no external garbage-collection' ([p.4](https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/16874549/Reversible_irreversible_and_optimal_machines.pdf#page=4)), and their JAM (jumping abstract machine) 'shortcuts redundant steps'.
sources.relevance: The closest existing answer to a core where nothing is recorded: a fixed reversible circuit, binary-tree tokens, copying as a tag. Costs: recomputation instead of sharing, and a single sequential token per query. The warning about additives (case analysis on constants) is aimed at triage.

sources.title: Reversible Combinatory Logic (Di Pierro, Hankin, Wiklicky, 2006)
sources.quote: This information is important to guarantee a unique replay of all reduction steps
sources.mechanism: rCL terms are pairs ⟨M | H⟩ over the basis B (bracketing), C (permutation), W (duplication) and K (deletion) (p.3). Each history entry records the rule plus two integers (where in the term the rule was applied, and the length of the prefix), so that replay is unique (p.5). K's entry also keeps the deleted term. Forward reduction is non-deterministic (any redex); backward reduction is deterministic (p.6). Example 3 (p.9) shows the history entries for W and B (W04, B10). Histories determine a group acting on reversible terms, the model is a groupoid, and rCL is 'universal for classical reversible computation' (p.2).
sources.relevance: The baseline design: an append-only log. K's entry carries data; W, B and C need only a label and a position. Global positions are the non-local part, which Nishida et al.'s root-only flattening removes.

sources.title: Reversible Computation in Term Rewriting (Nishida, Palacios, Vidal, 2018)
sources.quote: in which some information (namely, the positions where reduction takes place) is not required anymore
sources.mechanism: Reversible rewriting ⟨s, π⟩ ⇀ ⟨t, β(p, σ′) : π⟩. β is the rule label, p the position, and σ′ = σ restricted to Var(l)\Var(r), i.e. the bindings of erased variables only (p.8). Non-erasing rules store σ′ = id. Backward steps are deterministic. In pure constructor conditional systems (pcDCTRS), reached by flattening, every reduction happens at the topmost position, so positions are dropped. Injectivization makes each function return ⟨result, β(w…)⟩, and inversion builds f⁻¹. The improved injectivization (pp.31-32) drops the label β for a rule only when all three conditions hold: (1) its right-hand side does not overlap any other right-hand side of the same function; (2) it is non-erasing (Var(l) = Var(r)); (3) the right-hand side contains a single call to a defined function. 'Term rewriting is not reversible, even for injective functions' ([p.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1710.02804#page=1)).
sources.relevance: A formal recipe for tree calculus as rewriting: K stores z, the case split stores which branch (plus dropped arms), and S stores only its label. Undoing S matches a non-linear right-hand side, which is an equality check. The trace becomes a call-shaped tree returned beside the result, which matches the repo's `tc` (a repo claim).

sources.title: Reversible Computation and Reversible Programming Languages (Tetsuo Yokoyama, 2010)
sources.quote: The variable x on the left-hand side of an assignment must not appear in the expression e
sources.mechanism: Janus. The reversible update x ⊕= e uses ⊕ ∈ {+=, -=, ^=} (p.8). e may be any expression over other variables, including non-injective ones, so it maps (x, rest) to (x ⊕ e(rest), rest), and the opposite update undoes it. Swap x1 <=> x2 is sugar for three ^= updates (p.5). Conditional: if e1 then s1 else s2 fi e2, where the exit assertion makes it deterministic backwards: 'in the backward direction an assertion acts as a test and a test as an assertion' ([p.5](https://people.cs.rutgers.edu/~uli/cs516/spring2020/readings/ReversibleComputing-TheoreticalCompSci2010.pdf#page=5)). Loop: from e1 do s1 loop s2 until e2. Procedures can be run with call and uncall. fib returns a pair to make Fibonacci injective (p.2). Janus is not universal, but 'Janus with unbounded size stacks is r-Turing complete', meaning any reversible Turing machine can be simulated (p.9).
sources.relevance: (a) x ⊕= e(y) writes any function of y into x without history; copy is e = identity into a zeroed x. On trees this needs an invertible ⊕, which tree calculus lacks natively. (b) Exit assertions replace branch records whenever branch results are distinguishable.

sources.title: Semantics for a Turing-complete Reversible Programming Language with Inductive Types (Chardonnet, Lemonnier, Valiron, 2023)
sources.quote: build isos to encode notions of duplication, erasure, and constant manipulation thanks to partiality
sources.mechanism: Types 1, ⊕, ⊗ and inductive μX.A. Programs (isos) are sets of clauses. Variables are used linearly, and clauses must be 'non-overlapping on the left and on the right' ([p.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.12151#page=2)). Programs also have let, fix and higher-order iso variables. Dup_A : A ↔ A⊗A is defined by induction on the type (Def. 9, pp.6-7), and Lemma 11 shows Dup v →* ⟨v1, v2⟩ with v = v1 = v2. Its inverse, read off the clauses, only matches pairs with the same shape, i.e. equal pairs; this is inferred, not stated. erase_v = {⟨x, v⟩ ↔ x} erases a known constant (Def. 12). Any reversible Turing machine can be encoded. Every computable, partial, first-order injective function is realisable (completeness in PInj, the category of sets and partial injections). Semantics in join inverse rig categories.
sources.relevance: A small reversible primitive set over tree-shaped data in which copying and erasing known constants are derived, not primitive. On a lattice, a primitive layer-at-a-time Dup with its partial inverse may still be the right unit to price.

sources.title: The Zipper (Gérard Huet, 1997)
sources.quote: pointers from the root to the current position being reversed in a path structure
sources.mechanism: A location is (focus subtree, path), with path = Top | Node(left siblings, parent path, right siblings). go_left and go_right are mutual inverses. go_down moves to the leftmost child. go_up rebuilds the parent and forgets how many left siblings there were. So go_up∘go_down is the identity, but go_down∘go_up is the identity only from the leftmost child; up-moves are not injective. Navigation takes constant time 'except go_up, which is proportional to the juniority' (number of left siblings) (p.3). change, insert_* and delete edit at the focus and are not reversible (p.4). The path is the walk's history held as reversed pointers.
sources.relevance: A non-consuming reader: walk down, emit, walk back, leaving the tree in place, which is what Bennett's copy step needs. A history-free walk must ascend only from a known child position (e.g. walk left first), or keep a side tag in the path.

key_ideas: The losses in tree calculus are few and fixed. The building rules are already two-way. Jay's K deletes the third argument, his F rule decomposes the first and drops one, and S duplicates the third; undoing S needs an equality check, which is itself a tree-calculus program (Jay, Reflective Programs in Tree Calculus, pp.5, 40). Triage as a single rule is disp's variant, not the book's.

Keep the program when applying it: (f, x) → (f, f x). Then which rule fired and the untaken arms can be read off f, and only choices that depend on the data need recording. This rests on Axelsen and Glück's RTM-universality, whose exact (p, x) → (p, [[p]](x)) definition was not checkable from the fetched abstract.

Use exit assertions instead of records. A branch needs no record if its results are distinguishable (Janus's fi assertion; non-overlapping right sides in Chardonnet-Lemonnier-Valiron; biorthogonality in Abramsky). Otherwise store which branch was taken.

Record only erased bindings (Var(l)\Var(r)), and drop positions by rewriting only at the root of each call (Nishida-Palacios-Vidal). The trace becomes a call-shaped tree returned beside the result. A rule's label can be dropped only if its right side does not overlap, it erases nothing, and its right side makes a single defined-function call.

Copy is injective and its inverse is partial: Chardonnet et al.'s Dup has a clause inverse that only matches equal pairs. Janus's x -= y is total and leaves a residue unless x = y; partiality appears only where zero is asserted. Price copy and un-copy as matter in and out. Turning K drops into un-copies depends on the repo's measurement that most drops are of S-made copies.

The reversible update x ⊕= e(y), with e any expression not mentioning x (Janus), writes any function of y into a zeroed x with no history, and copying is e = identity. On trees this needs an invertible ⊕, which tree calculus does not have natively.

Reuse circuits instead of copying them. Abramsky's replication !f puts the copy index in the token as p(t, ·), so one circuit serves every copy. K is affine: dropping is free when the token never enters the dropped argument.

Walking without history (Lange-McKenzie-Tapp Euler tour, the interaction machine of the geometry of interaction, Morita's rotary element) uses no extra space but pays in time and runs sequentially. Parallelism comes only from independent queries, which need no synchronization (Dal Lago et al.). A Huet zipper is only partly history-free: going up forgets which child you came from unless you always ascend from a known position.

A price ladder for history: Bennett 1973 (linear time, one record per step) → Bennett 1989 (time T^(1+ε), space S log T) → Lange-McKenzie-Tapp (exponential time, space S). Simulations that obey Bennett's pebble rule need the log T factor (LMT p.2), so a local pebble rule alone cannot beat S log T.

Bennett's history entries are bare transition indices because a Turing-machine step forgets a bounded, rule-determined symbol. Tree-calculus K forgets an unbounded subtree, so its record must carry data (Di Pierro et al., Nishida et al.).
For one-to-one programs, the inverse's history is what erases the input (Bennett 1973 stages 4-7; Bennett 1989 Theorem 2 and Table 3), so such a program can finish with nothing left over.
A particle moving through 1-bit rotary elements (Morita) is clock-free, particle-conserving and garbage-free. It can be embedded in a reversible cellular automaton (P3), and it is sequential.

Abramsky's boundary: the multiplicative-exponential part of linear logic (where the pure λ-calculus lives) is reversible. Adding constants with a conditional (the additives) loses partial injectivity. Triage, a case split on shape, sits on that boundary.

field: Spatial and chemical models of computation: artificial chemistries (AlChemy, combinator chemistries, chemlambda/chemSKI), the chemical abstract machine, graph-rewriting automata, the Movable Feast Machine, amorphous computing, lattice chemistries (Squirm3, spatial program soups), plus the two physics anchors these lean on (Bennett's Brownian/enzymatic computers, Margolus's partitioned reversible CA). Read against disp's nine criteria for a reversible, linear, lattice-based tree-calculus core.

sources.title: The Barrier of Objects: From Dynamical Systems to Bounded Organizations (IIASA WP-96-027; covers AlChemy = 'Minimal Chemistry Zero', MC1, MC2)
sources.quote: atom types and number are conserved during a reaction event
sources.mechanism: AlChemy (MC0) is a well-stirred flow reactor of N lambda terms. Two terms A and B collide, (A)B is reduced to normal form C, and the reaction is A + B -> C + A + B, so reactants are not used up ([p.17](https://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/4999/1/WP-96-027.pdf#page=17): 'Reactants are not used up in a reaction'). After each new product, a randomly chosen expression is removed so N stays exactly constant. That global random removal is the only outflow. Organisation levels, as summarised here: 'Level 0' means hypercycles, i.e. structures that sustain themselves only through copy actions (fixed points such as (g)f = f). 'Level 1' appears when replicators are disabled, or when their copying is mixed with constructive interactions: self-maintaining sets that produce each other, with self-repair and extensibility. Combining independently obtained organisations gives higher-order organisations held together by a 'glue' set. MC1 adds simple types to model shape (selective binding). MC2 is explicitly 'yet to be implemented': molecules are proofs in multiplicative linear logic, a reaction is a cut between dual sites, and cut elimination is the reaction, which is symmetric. The paper's resource-accountability critique of MC0/MC1 notes that a repeated variable uses one reactant twice ([p.24](https://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/4999/1/WP-96-027.pdf#page=24), 'Where does the second 5 come from?'), and that an unused bound variable 'annihilates' a reactant (p.38 of the PDF). History: none. Each collision is one opaque, irreversible normalisation.
sources.relevance: The diagnosis carries over to tree calculus almost word for word. The S rule's duplicated z is 'the second 5', and K and triage are the 'annihilated reactant'. A conserving tree chemistry therefore needs exactly two ledgers: S imports a second z, and K and triage export what they drop. Warning: cheap copying lets trivial copiers dominate. In this paper that shows up as hypercycles (Level 0). The 2024 re-run makes it concrete as identity-function copiers ([Return to AlChemy, p.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.12137#page=4): 'This occurs because the function of copying any input is trivial in'). MC2's 'reaction = cut between dual sites' is the interaction-net active pair, but MC2 was never run, so it supports the shape only, not any results.

sources.title: The Chemical Abstract Machine
sources.quote: any number of reactions can be performed in parallel, provided that they involve disjoint sets of molecules
sources.mechanism: The state is a solution: a multiset of molecules. A specific CHAM is a molecule syntax plus rewrite rules on sub-multisets. All CHAMs obey four general laws ([p.11](https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs522/sp2016/TheChemicalAbstractMachine.pdf#page=11)). Reaction law: a rule instance is replaced by its right side. Chemical law: reactions can be performed freely in any solution, so disjoint ones commute. Membrane law: a subsolution evolves freely in any context. Airlock law: a reversible way to pull one molecule out of a membrane so it can interact. Heating/cooling rules break a molecule into parts and reassemble it, and they play the role of structural equivalence ([p.3](https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs522/sp2016/TheChemicalAbstractMachine.pdf#page=3)). Reaction rules are one-way, e.g. CCS communication ([p.5](https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs522/sp2016/TheChemicalAbstractMachine.pdf#page=5): 'Unlike the parallel rule, the reaction rule is irreversible'). Inert 0 molecules are removed by a cleanup rule ('0 evaporates when heated', p.6). The paper admits a CHAM can loop, heating and cooling back and forth (p.7). Copying or erasure only happens if a rule's right side duplicates or drops something. There is no history.
sources.relevance: It gives disp vocabulary for two classes of moves. Strand and wire moves (diffusion, rewiring, reshaping a path) are 'heating/cooling': reversible bookkeeping. The tree-calculus rules are 'reactions': the only one-way moves. The chemical law states criterion 2 precisely: any reactions on disjoint material may fire, with no scheduler. Membrane plus airlock is a reversible attach/detach of one molecule to a bounded region, an analogy for an apply agent docking on a tree and undocking. The CHAM says nothing about energy, so 'energy-neutral vs priced' is disp's own reading, not the paper's.

sources.title: Two-State Graph-Rewriting Automata (talk slides; summarises Graph automata: natural expression of self-reproduction, Physica D 171, 2002)
sources.quote: node rules (trans, div) at even time
sources.mechanism: These are cellular automata on a dynamic 3-link planar graph ('Not restricted on lattice space', [p.3](https://www.wolframscience.com/conference/2006/presentations/materials/tomita.pdf#page=3)). Each node has a finite state. Node rules: trans x,(a,b,c)->y changes a node's state from its own and its three neighbours' states, and div x,(a,b,c)->y replaces a node by a triangle of three nodes. The general form also has fus, the inverse of div. Link rules: com(x,y) rewires the link between two nodes (an edge flip), and anh(x,y) deletes two linked nodes and reconnects their remaining links, which can separate the graph. Updates are synchronous, with node rules at even steps and link rules at odd steps, and lateral inhibition to stop neighbouring link rules from colliding. An asynchronous version simulates this by adding local synchronisation states ([p.35](https://www.wolframscience.com/conference/2006/presentations/materials/tomita.pdf#page=35)). An exhaustive search over two-state rule sets (11-digit codes, 1,769,472 of them) finds self-replicating graphs. Hand-built many-state rule sets give a self-replicating TM (20 states, 257 rules) and Minsky's small UTM with self-reproduction (30 states/955 rules to reproduce plus 23 states/745 rules to compute) ([p.34](https://www.wolframscience.com/conference/2006/presentations/materials/tomita.pdf#page=34)). Nothing is conserved and there is no history.
sources.relevance: This shows directly that whole-machine self-reproduction works with purely local rules on degree-3 graphs, the same shape as disp's interaction nets. It separates 'rewire' (com) from 'create/annihilate' (div/anh). Mapping disp's Dn to div and Eps to anh, and pricing those two while strand moves stay free, is our design reading. Its weak point is that it has no spatial embedding (the slides list 'embed in 3D space' only for visualisation), which the strand lattice addresses.

sources.title: Pursue robust indefinite scalability (the Movable Feast Machine)
sources.quote: Computation in the MFM is based on event windows
sources.mechanism: The hardware model is an open-ended grid of tiles. Each tile holds 48x48 sites, and each site holds one 64-bit atom (element type, bonds, data). A bond is a distance-limited, symmetric, self-relative pointer: long bonds have L1 <= 4, short bonds L1 <= 2. An event picks a centre site in a 'hardware-dependent but starvation-free manner' and exclusively holds the window: the centre plus its radius-4 neighbourhood. The element's loop-free update code reads and writes only inside that window. Afterwards the atom is diffused to a random von Neumann neighbour site, if that does not overextend a bond. 'An indefinite number of nonoverlapping windows may occur in parallel.' A 'DReg' element mostly diffuses, but sometimes deletes a nearby atom or creates a Res (resource) atom or another DReg, so structures must repair or reproduce. Unregulated reproduction 'would amount to cancer', but if components 'reproduce only by transmuting existing Res atoms' then DReg regulates their density too ([p.4](https://www.cs.unm.edu/~ackley/papers/hotos-11.pdf#page=4)). 'Opportunistic reproduction for parallelism and robustness' is a stated design strategy (p.2). Examples include a self-healing wire, cell membranes, sorting, a movable NAND gate and a simple stack machine interpreter. There is no conservation or reversibility.
sources.relevance: This is the existing system closest to the repo's strand lattice: sites, short relative-pointer bonds, random local events, and diffusion limited by bonds. (a) Copying should consume a local resource species, and that species' density then regulates how far self-reproduction spreads: the 'copy draws fuel' rule, and the paper's own anti-cancer argument. (b) Non-overlapping event windows give the same disjointness guarantee as disp's 2x2x2 blocks. The difference is that MFM picks windows asynchronously and at random, while Margolus-style blocks use a fixed alternating partition. The analogy covers disjointness only, not scheduling.

sources.title: Amorphous Computing (MIT AI Memo 1665)
sources.quote: A growing point is an activity of a group of neighboring computational particles that can be propagated to an overlapping neighborhood
sources.mechanism: Many unreliable particles, interconnected in 'unknown, irregular, and time-varying ways', with local state and only local communication. The primitives are diffusion waves carrying hop counts, which estimate distance from a source ([p.4](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/mac/projects/amorphous/papers/aim1665.pdf#page=4)), regions grown by bounding the hop count, and Coore's growing points. A growing point propagates through neighbouring particles. It can split, die off or merge. It may have a tropism toward or away from 'pheromones' secreted by particles of particular materials. As it passes, it 'may permanently set some portion of the states of the particles it visits', which the memo reads as laying down a material. Robustness comes from redundancy. There is no copy or erase accounting, and gradients are free broadcast.
sources.relevance: The growing point is a precedent for an agent that leaves a persistent trail of state behind as it moves. In disp the trail is the strand path, and we would like it to serve as wire, history and way back. The memo supports only the 'trail of laid-down material' part. Using the trail as history, and undoing by retracting along it, is our extension, not something the memo proposes. The free broadcast (gradients) has to be dropped or priced to stay linear.

sources.title: Combinatory Chemistry: Towards a Simple Model of Emergent Evolution
sources.quote: S duplicates its third argument x. Thus, to make a chemical system with conservation laws
sources.mechanism: A multiset P of SKI expressions, initialised with elementary combinators only. Reduce reactions carry by-products in brackets: I: a(I f)b -> a f b [+I]. K: a(K f g)b -> a f b [+g +K]. S: a(S f g x)b [+x] -> a(f x (g x))b [+S]. K releases the dropped argument g and the spent K into the pool instead of deleting them. An S redex is only reducible if a copy of x (the 'reactant') is present in P. That copy is removed from P, and the spent S is released. So S, K and I atom counts are invariant. If an expression has no redex, it is either cleaved at a random point or condensed with another irreducible expression ([p.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.07916#page=3): 'Otherwise, if an expression cannot be reduced, it is either cleaved at a random point, or condensed together with another irreducible expression'). Reductions take priority. Emergent structures include self-maintaining metabolic cycles and the recursively growing (AA) with A = S(SI)I: '(AA) + 3A -> 2(AA) + phi(A)', which 'creates a copy of itself from 2 freely available units of A and metabolises a third one' ([p.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2003.07916#page=5)). The paper notes that S reduction is the only operation through which an expression incorporates a reactant into its body. A longer follow-up ([arXiv 2103.08245](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.08245)) reports self-reproducing metabolisms emerging from a tabula rasa start.
sources.relevance: This is a near-literal template for a conserving tree chemistry. Count application nodes as nodes. Then tree-calculus S, △(△x)y z -> x z (y z) (the treecalcul.us form the repo uses; Jay's book writes y z (x z), and the count is the same), turns fork + stem + apply into three applies. It is therefore node-neutral except for the second z. K and triage release their dropped subtrees and spent nodes. So the whole ledger is: S needs a z reactant, and K/triage emit by-products. On a lattice the pool must be local, so the z reactant has to be built next to the redex by a duplicator drawing on a local free-node gas. Matching by value (any equal copy of x will do) is what the paper does in a well-mixed pool; on a lattice it needs a local equality test.

sources.title: chemSKI with tokens: world building and economy in the SKI universe (with Project Hapax)
sources.quote: In order to be conservative in nodes and edges, we need to add tokens
sources.mechanism: Graphs use nodes I and K (1-valent), S (3-valent, also used as a fan-out), A (application), Arrow, and FRIN/FROUT, written as 'mol' lines. Every rewrite is local between two nodes. Example K-A: LHS 'K 1, A 1 a 2, A 2 b c' -> RHS 'K e, Arrow a c, Arrow b e'. The dropped b is wired to a K, which then prunes it through TERMINATION-kind rewrites (I-A, I-S, K-S, S-K, A-K). COMB removes Arrow nodes. With tokens added on both sides (A-A, I-A, S-A, S-K, S-S, Arrow), 'RHS with tokens' is a permutation of 'LHS with tokens'. For K-A that is the explicit permutation (0 e 2 1 b 3 6 5 c 7 a 4 9 d 8 f). Each token carries 1 to 3 unique edge names. The cost of a rewrite is cost[Out Tokens] - cost[In Tokens], and token prices are left to the application (names carried, scarcity, or trading). 'Dirty' quines accumulate inert waste graphs, with cost[Initial] + InCost = cost[Final] + OutCost and OutCost = Profit + cost[waste]. Token, synthesis (copy/erase) and waste-recycling rewrites are proposed, but 'In this version of the programs these rewrites are not implemented.' Hapax states the general scheme as '(LEFT PATTERN) + (TOKEN_1) + (ENZYME) = (RIGHT PATTERN) + (TOKEN_2) + (ENZYME)', with a graph rewrite encoded 'as a permutation of the ends of the edges of a graph', and 14400 variants of the beta rewrite ([hapax README](https://github.com/mbuliga/hapax#goal-of-hapax)).
sources.relevance: This is the most direct answer to criteria 4 and 5. Write each tree-calculus rule as 'block + tokens_in' -> a permutation of the same slots -> 'block' + tokens_out'. Each 2x2x2 lattice move is then a bijection that conserves nodes and wire ends, and the energy is the token-cost difference. The claim that heat is the information in which typed token came out is our interpretation; chemSKI defines cost only as a scalar per token type. The Hapax ENZYME appears unchanged on both sides, so structurally it is a catalyst. The README does not explain it further, so 'a circuit reused rather than copied' is our extrapolation.

sources.title: Chemlambda, universality and self-multiplication
sources.quote: provide the mechanism of selfmultiplication of molecules, together with the FAN-IN move
sources.mechanism: Locally planar graphs built from lambda, fan-out, application and fan-in nodes, plus arrows, loops and termination nodes. Moves: graphic beta, FAN-IN, the DIST moves, and local pruning moves (p.4). The DIST moves (a fan-out meeting a lambda or application node and being pushed through it) together with FAN-IN make molecules self-multiply. Chemlambda 'was introduced in order to eliminate this unpleasant GLOBAL FAN-OUT' of graphic lambda calculus, and uses only local moves. Computation is 'asynchronous, purely local and decentralized' application of these rewrites, and the molecules are not embedded in any space. The companion paper ([arXiv 2005.06060, p.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.06060#page=2)) says the rewrites can be done by a local machine that is also 'local in time, in the sense that the algorithm can retain only a limited in time portion of the history', using a random rewrite algorithm. There is no conservation in this version.
sources.relevance: This is the precedent for disp's layer-at-a-time duplicator. Copying a whole program becomes a local front of DIST moves rather than one global step, so a copy and its consumers can overlap (copy-ahead). The 'local in time' result means a simulator needs only a bounded window of recent history. That is consistent with keeping history only near the activity, but the paper is about simulation memory, not about reversibility.

sources.title: Evolvable Self-Replicating Molecules in an Artificial Chemistry (Squirm3)
sources.quote: A move to a square is valid if the atom remains within the neighbourhood of every atom it is bonded with
sources.mechanism: A 2D grid with at most one atom per square. Each atom has a fixed type a-f and a mutable state. Bonds are formed and broken by reactions. Each step an atom moves to an empty Moore-neighbour square or stays, but only if it stays adjacent to every atom it is bonded to. Reactions happen between von Neumann neighbours and depend only on the two atoms' types, states and whether they are bonded. Table 1 ([p.5](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~turk/bio_sim/articles/hutton_rep_molecules.pdf#page=5)) has eight reactions, e.g. R1 e8 + e0 -> e4e3 (bond), R2 x4y1 -> x2y5, R6 f4f3 -> f8 + f8 and R8 x9y9 -> x8 + y8 (unbond). With them any chain e8-(a|b|c|d)1...-f1 copies itself by templating from a soup of state-0 free atoms, and R6-R8 split the chain from its copy. Replication stalls when a needed free atom type runs out: in a run, 'stuck halfway because there aren't any b0's left' ([p.6](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~turk/bio_sim/articles/hutton_rep_molecules.pdf#page=6)). The reaction set is 'dirty': a flaw in R4 lets chains cross over and produce new replicators. Atoms are never created or destroyed by reactions. In the evolution experiment, though, half the world is periodically wiped and refilled with fresh state-0 atoms ([p.8](https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~turk/bio_sim/articles/hutton_rep_molecules.pdf#page=8)).
sources.relevance: This is template copying on a lattice whose bonds constrain movement, the same picture as the repo's strands. It shows a duplicator can be a zipper running along a strand, recruiting free atoms of the right type from the local gas. Raw-material scarcity is then a built-in brake on self-reproduction, as the paper observed. Each recruitment step is a small pairwise state change, so it could in principle be made a bijection that carries fuel/refund accounting, but Squirm3 itself does not do this.

sources.title: Computational Life: How Well-formed, Self-replicating Programs Emerge from Simple Interaction
sources.quote: Where exec runs the concatenated programs and split divides the result back into two 64 byte strings
sources.mechanism: A soup of fixed-size 64-byte programs in BFF, a self-modifying Brainfuck variant with byte-copy instructions. A reaction is A + B -> split(exec(AB)) = A' + B': concatenate two tapes, run them for a fixed number of steps or until they end, and cut back into two 64-byte tapes. Background mutation is also applied, but the paper reports replicators arise even without it. Total memory is conserved, and copying overwrites the partner's bytes. Self-replicators emerge from random tapes with no fitness function, detected by a state transition in 'high-order entropy'. Spatial variant: 32,400 programs on a 240x135 grid, where 'two programs can only interact if their distance is at most 2 along each coordinate' ([p.9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.19108#page=9)). Each epoch visits programs in random order, pairs each with a random neighbour if neither is already taken, then runs all taken pairs, so each epoch's pairs are disjoint. Forth on a 2D grid and Z80 CPUs on a 2D grid also produce self-replicator ecosystems.
sources.relevance: 'Collide, run, split' is a material-conserving pairwise reaction. Copying here destroys the partner's information by overwriting it, at no cost, which is where a heat charge would belong in a physical version. It also shows empirically that cheap copying plus locality ends with replicators filling memory. If disp uses self-reproduction for parallelism, copying must be throttled by fuel.

sources.title: The thermodynamics of computation - a review
sources.quote: The reaction catalyzed by RNA polymerase is reversible: sometimes the enzyme takes up a free pyrophosphate molecule
sources.mechanism: A Brownian computer is a thermal random walk on the computation's state graph, biased forward by a weak driving force, and its drift velocity is linear in the dissipation per step. The concrete example is RNA polymerase as a Brownian tape copier. A forward step adds a complementary nucleotide and releases pyrophosphate. The reverse step takes pyrophosphate up and removes the end nucleotide. At equilibrium both steps occur equally often, and in cells the supply of triphosphates and removal of pyrophosphate drive it forward at about 20kT per nucleotide (p.10). The hypothetical enzymatic Turing machine (p.11-13) has a macromolecular tape with symbols and a head marker, and 'several hypothetical enzymes (one for each of the Turing machine's transition rules)'. Each enzyme is readied for reuse through coupling to an external reaction (e.g. ATP), which drives the walk ([Fig. 6, p.13](https://fab.cba.mit.edu/classes/863.18/notes/computation/Bennett-1982.pdf#page=13)). The machine must be logically reversible, or the walk bogs down among extraneous predecessors unless about kT ln 2 is dissipated at each merge. Reversibility can be bought with a history tape that is later un-computed, after copying the output.
sources.relevance: It gives the economics asked for in criterion 6. Copying draws fuel (monomers), un-copying returns it, and the direction is set by local concentrations, not a controller. In disp, Dn's Metropolis acceptance could depend on local free-node concentration, a chemical potential; that is our proposal, not Bennett's. 'One enzyme per transition rule' is the model for reusing a rule-circuit instead of copying it. Note, though, that Bennett's enzymes are not free catalysts: each cycle is reset by coupling to an external fuel reaction.

sources.title: Physics-like models of computation
sources.quote: embody discrete analogues of the classical-physics notions of space, time, locality, and microscopic reversibility
sources.mechanism: Partitioning cellular automata. The lattice is divided into 2x2 blocks, each treated as a 4-input/4-output conservative-logic gate, and the blocking alternates between a solid and a dotted partition on successive steps ([p.5](https://fab.cba.mit.edu/classes/862.16/notes/computation/Margolus-1984.pdf#page=5)). If the block rule maps distinct block states to distinct states, the global step is invertible ([p.6](https://fab.cba.mit.edu/classes/862.16/notes/computation/Margolus-1984.pdf#page=6): 'Since each distinct initial state of a block is mapped onto a distinct final state, this rule is reversible'). The billiard-ball (BBM) rule is also conservative, preserving the number of 1s and 0s, and it simulates Fredkin's billiard ball model, so it is computation-universal. Second-order RCA (the next state is a function of the current neighbourhood combined with the previous state, mod k) are reversible for any function, because the previous state is carried along. The paper discusses entropy in RCA and conserved quantities such as moving 'dislocations'.
sources.relevance: The repo's 2x2x2 block moves are this partitioning lifted to 3D. If every block move is a permutation of the block's contents plus tokens (the chemSKI construction), the whole lattice is reversible by construction. Metropolis acceptance then becomes a detailed-balance choice among bijections; that framing is ours. This is the bridge from the space-free chemistries above to a substrate that could run on reversible hardware.

key_ideas: A node-conserving tree chemistry has only two unbalanced rules. Count application nodes as nodes. S, △(△x)y z -> x z (y z) (treecalcul.us form; Jay's book has y z (x z), and the count is the same), turns fork + stem + apply into three applies, so it is node-neutral except that it needs a second z. K, △△y z -> y, and triage release what they drop plus the spent nodes. So the whole ledger is: S imports a z reactant, and K/triage emit by-products. (Kruszewski & Mikolov 2020 by-product brackets; Fontana & Buss 1996 'second 5' and 'annihilated reactant' critique)

Replace erasure with release, and charge heat only when a released piece is taken apart. A subtree dropped by K or triage stays an intact, known molecule nearby. Only when it is dismantled into indistinguishable free nodes is its shape information lost, and that is where heat is paid. This is a design proposal: the sources supply the release (Kruszewski & Mikolov), explicit waste with a cost balance and proposed but unimplemented waste-recycling rewrites (chemSKI), and the erasure-cost principle (Bennett). None of them states the 'heat only on dismantling' rule.

Every rule as a permutation of a bounded block. Add token molecules to both sides of each tree-calculus rule, so that 'block + tokens in' is a permutation of 'block + tokens out' on the half-edge slots of a 2x2x2 block. Each lattice move is then a bijection that conserves nodes and wire ends, and the energy is the token-cost difference. Tokens carry their own fresh edge names (1 to 3 each), so no global id supply is needed. (Buliga chemSKI-with-tokens and Hapax; Margolus partitioning with alternating blockings)

Copy by templating from a local raw-material gas. The duplicator zips along a strand and recruits free nodes from adjacent sites, one per step. The reverse step (un-copy) returns them. Direction and speed are set by local free-node concentration, a chemical potential that would enter disp's Metropolis energy; that last part is our proposal. Scarcity throttles self-reproduction, as observed in Squirm3, where replication stalls when b0 atoms run out. (Bennett 1982 RNA polymerase; Hutton Squirm3; Ackley 'reproduce only by transmuting existing Res atoms')

Two move classes. Wire and strand rearrangements are reversible bookkeeping, like CHAM heating/cooling, the com edge flip, and the div/fus pair in graph-rewriting automata. Only the tree-calculus reactions and copy/release are one-way or priced; the pricing is our addition, since the CHAM assigns no cost. Disjoint reactions commute, which says 'everything ready fires at once' needs no scheduler. (Berry & Boudol chemical law; Tomita com vs div/anh; Ackley non-overlapping event windows)

Reuse circuits through catalysts, not copies. A function applied many times could act as an enzyme that appears on both sides of a reaction, docking, acting and undocking. Parallelism then comes from a population of such catalysts rather than one code copy per call. Caveat from Bennett: enzymes are re-readied each cycle by coupling to an external fuel reaction, so reuse still costs per use. Hapax's ENZYME is on both sides of the scheme but is otherwise unexplained. (Hapax README; Bennett one enzyme per transition rule; Ackley opportunistic reproduction; Tomita self-reproducing universal TM)

History as a trail in space (design proposal). A moving agent leaves its strand path behind; that path is its wire, its history and its way back, and undoing is retracting along it. The sources support the parts: growing points 'permanently set' state along their path (amorphous computing), and chemlambda's simulator needs only a bounded recent window of history ('local in time'). Neither uses the trail for reversal.

Waste of one reaction is the reactant of another. Released subtrees can serve as S-reactants elsewhere, so a computation can pay for its copies with its own earlier drops. Metabolisms such as (AA) + 3A -> 2(AA) + phi(A) arise unprompted from elementary combinators. (Kruszewski & Mikolov 2020; Fontana & Buss organisations)

Throttle copying or it becomes cancer. In systems with cheap copying, copiers dominate: AlChemy's Level 0 hypercycles (Fontana & Buss), identity-function copiers in the 2024 AlChemy re-run (Mathis et al.), and BFF replicators filling the grid (Agüera y Arcas et al. 2024). Ackley uses the word 'cancer' and fixes it by letting components reproduce only by transmuting Res atoms. So fuel-priced copying is a correctness condition for parallelism-by-reproduction.

field: Linearity, copying and deletion as resources: no-cloning and no-deleting, what copying costs when done reversibly (fanout onto a blank), the linear-logic exponentials and their bounded and light variants, optimal sharing, reference counting and in-place reuse, garbage-free duplication in reversible languages, and erasure as an explicit, priced effect (Landauer)

sources.title: Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process (Landauer 1961)
sources.quote: logically irreversible if the output of a device does not uniquely define the inputs
sources.mechanism: A bit is a particle in a double-well potential. RESTORE TO ONE (reset/erase) sends both states to one; the entropy lost by the bits must appear elsewhere as heat, at least 0.6931 kT per restored bit (p.5). A device is logically irreversible if its output does not determine its input (p.4). An irreversible function can be embedded in a reversible one, but the machine then needs 'extra capacity to store both the extra "bias" bits and the extra outputs' ([p.4](https://worrydream.com/refs/Landauer_1961_-_Irreversibility_and_Heat_Generation_in_the_Computing_Process.pdf#page=4)). For a nonterminating program that capacity 'cannot be there' (p.4), so the stored garbage must eventually be erased, and that erasure is where the heat goes (p.6).
sources.relevance: Gives disp's ledger its heat unit and says where heat may appear: only at many-to-one maps. The tree-calculus reading (leaf/stem application and the S rule are one-to-one, K and triage are many-to-one, so only these two can be heat sources, priced by information actually lost rather than agents removed) is disp's own analysis, not something Landauer says.

sources.title: Logical Reversibility of Computation (Bennett 1973)
sources.quote: the history tape is not random - there exists a subtle mutual redundancy between it and the machine
sources.mechanism: A reversible three-tape Turing machine whose transitions are one-to-one, with read/write and shift steps split apart. Stage 1 runs the ordinary machine and writes the index of each transition on a history tape. Stage 2 copies the output onto a blank output tape (reversible because that tape is blank) while history recording is suspended. Stage 3 runs stage 1 backward, consuming the history tape back to blank. What remains is the input plus the output, with no garbage. Cost: 'about twice as many steps as on an ordinary one' plus n history records for an n-step first stage. The quoted sentence continues: the redundancy 'may be exploited to erase it reversibly'.
sources.relevance: The shape a reversible disp run should keep: run forward leaving residue, copy the answer onto blanks, then run the local rules backward to consume the residue. The disp-specific change is to keep history as local particles left where K/triage dropped things instead of a central numbered log. History space can be cut with Bennett's pebbling, which [Li & Vitányi](https://arxiv.org/pdf/quant-ph/9703022#page=1) show uses the least extra space among pebble-game simulations (time roughly T^log2(3) for space S log T; verified: 'for k = 2 we have ǫ = log 3', p.6).

sources.title: Notes on Landauer's Principle, Reversible Computation, and Maxwell's Demon (Bennett 2003)
sources.quote: copying unknown data onto a blank (ie initially zero) register, and the reverse process
sources.mechanism: Bennett names two key logically reversible operations on a register pair (x, y): copying x into y when y is initially zero, and erasing y to zero when x and y are known to be equal; 'for any initial values of x and y the two operations are' restrictions of a bijection (the XOR / CNOT form). Erasing data that is random is a thermodynamically reversible transfer of entropy to the environment (kT ln 2 per bit). Applying a logically irreversible operation to known data is thermodynamically irreversible, because the environmental entropy increase is not compensated; this 'wasteful situation' can be avoided. Any computation that saves a copy of its input can be globally reprogrammed as logically reversible steps (p.4).
sources.relevance: disp's price list (copying draws fuel, un-copy refunds, erasing unique information makes heat) matches this. The open engineering problem is witnessing 'known to be identical' locally: structurally (the duplicator still links both copies, as in interaction-combinator annihilation) or by comparison (an Rfun-style dup/eq agent). The XOR form shows fanout is a special case of 'add onto'.

sources.title: Impossibility of deleting an unknown quantum state (Pati & Braunstein 2000)
sources.quote: Classically we may delete one copy against the others, uncopying it in a perfectly reversible manner
sources.mechanism: Suppose a linear machine maps |psi>|psi>|A> to |psi>|Sigma>|A_psi> for every psi. Applying it to |H>|H>, |V>|V> and a superposition, linearity plus normalization forces the ancilla states A_H and A_V to be orthogonal, so the machine 'is therefore not uncopying at all, but merely swapping onto a two-dimensional subspace of the ancilla' (p.2). The paper explicitly excludes swapping as deletion (p.2). Together with no-cloning, copying and uncopying are meaningful only in a fixed basis.
sources.relevance: For a quantum substrate, the duplicator and un-copy must be computational-basis operations; trees stay classical data. A superposition agent meeting a duplicator yields entanglement, not two copies. Un-copy should be modelled as the inverse of a bijective fanout, never as deletion of an unknown state.

sources.title: Interaction Combinators (Lafont 1997; mirror of the author's PostScript)
sources.quote: commutation when the two cells carry different symbols
sources.mechanism: Three agents: γ (constructor, arity 2), δ (duplicator, arity 2), ε (eraser, arity 0). Six rules: commutation when the cells differ (γδ, γε, δε) and annihilation when they match (γγ, δδ, εε). Annihilation removes both agents and reconnects auxiliary wires; γ meeting δ gives 2 γ + 2 δ; ε meeting γ or δ gives two ε. Each rule consumes 2 agents and makes at most 4. Strongly deterministic: 'not only the result, but also the computation is unique, up to trivial commutations' ([p.2](https://dcreager.net/pdf/Lafont1997.pdf#page=2)). Universal: 'only three symbols and six rules, is a universal model of distributed computation' ([p.1](https://dcreager.net/pdf/Lafont1997.pdf#page=1)). Annihilation rules are 'disconnected' and so not locally invertible ([Salikhmetov p.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07275#page=4)).
sources.relevance: The repo's Dn, Eps and labelled Sup agents are δ, ε and labelled δ. disp could price per rule kind (δ commutation draws fuel, δδ annihilation refunds it, ε reaching a leaf is the heat event) and use 3 agents / 6 rules as the bar for 'simpler than now'. Those prices are a disp proposal; Lafont prices nothing.

sources.title: Light Linear Logic (Girard 1998; section 1.1 recaps Bounded Linear Logic)
sources.quote: still valid w.r.t. bounded exponentials : the bounds are respectively given by 0, 1, +
sources.mechanism: BLL (Girard, Scedrov, Scott) replaces !A ('A ad libitum') by (1&A)⊗...⊗(1&A), a finite tensor power !_n A: an n-use licence. Weakening, dereliction, contraction and promotion stay valid with bounds 0, 1, + and · respectively. LLL instead drops dereliction and digging (principles [VI], [VII] 'definitely excluded', p.4), adds the neutral modality § as a compensation, and restricts promotion's context, giving polynomial-time cut-elimination at fixed depth.
sources.relevance: (a) A duplicator could carry a copy budget n that contraction splits additively and weakening returns, giving a local static fuel bound per shared value. (b) Stratification is what makes optimal sharing local. (c) Dereliction and digging are where unbounded copying comes from, so they mark where prices belong. All three are disp proposals built on BLL/LLL.

sources.title: Light Logics and Optimal Reduction: Completeness and Complexity (Baillot, Coppola, Dal Lago 2007)
sources.quote: without the so-called oracle, so plain graph rewriting with local rules
sources.mechanism: Abstract sharing graphs (Fig. 6) have λ, @, fan_i (with an integer index) and a weakening node. @ meeting λ annihilates; fans with equal index annihilate, unequal indices commute; fans duplicate λ and @ nodes. Garbage-collection rules are omitted, which the authors argue is harmless (p.6). EAL/LAL proof nets translate by turning contractions into fans indexed by a labelling function compatible with box depths, then deleting boxes. For EAL- (LAL-) typable terms Lamping's abstract algorithm (no oracle) is sound and complete with an elementary (polynomial) bound. Asperti later summarises Asperti et al. 2004: the non-elementary cost of optimal reduction 'is not due to bookkeeping ... but to the (apparently unavoidable) duplication work' ([p.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.04240#page=5)).
sources.relevance: The formal answer to 'when does sharing beat copying': share by default, copy a node only when a fan reaches it, un-copy when matching fans meet. Labels that are levels make un-copy a local decision. The S rule (two copies later applied to each other's results) is where static levels plausibly break, and the repo's dynamic Sup labels are the HVM-style workaround; that diagnosis is disp's, not the paper's.

sources.title: A Structural Approach to Reversible Computation (Abramsky 2005)
sources.quote: The purpose of the replication operation described previously is precisely to make the argument copyable
sources.mechanism: Models are biorthogonal pattern-matching automata: A and A^op are both orthogonal, rules are linear (same variables on both sides), so computation is step-by-step reversible (p.6). Terms denote partial injections (realised as partial involutions). Replication: !f = {(p(t,u), p(t,v)) | t ∈ TΣ, (u,v) ∈ f}: no copies are made; tag t says which copy. Linear application: LApp(f,g) = f_rr ∪ f_rl;g;(f_ll;g)*;f_lr (p.11). This gives a linear combinatory algebra and so universality for pure combinatory logic, with automaton size linear in the term (p.1). Multiplicative-exponential structure is handled reversibly but 'this fails for the additives' ([p.25](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=25)).
sources.relevance: Draws the line between reversible and irreversible: K and S can be reversible for free when circuits are re-used, so the irreversible core is case analysis on data (triage). This is the theory behind the deleted iso Machine. Danos and Regnier make the same point for interaction machines: the word 'will sometimes grow and sometimes shrink. It needs no external garbage-collection' ([p.4](https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/16874549/Reversible_irreversible_and_optimal_machines.pdf#page=4)).

sources.title: Join Inverse Rig Categories for Reversible Functional Programming, and Beyond (Kaarsgaard & Rennela 2021; primer on Rfun)
sources.quote: To allow for (de)duplication of values, a special duplication/equality operator
sources.mechanism: Rfun has linear variables (each bound variable used exactly once in the body, p.2), constructor terms, and case expressions under the symmetric first-match policy (p.2). It is r-Turing complete: it 'can simulate any reversible Turing machine' (p.3). Because linearity blocks duplication, a special duplication/equality operator ⌊·⌋ is added (Fig. 1): ⌊<x>⌋ = <x,x>; ⌊<x,y>⌋ = <x> if x = y, and <x,y> otherwise. It is its own inverse and can be used both as a value and as a pattern (p.3).
sources.relevance: iso.rs's Dup, whose inverse applies only to equal halves, is a partial ⌊⌋. Rfun shows how to make it total and self-inverse by passing unequal pairs through. On the lattice it would be a zipper agent comparing two trees layer by layer, re-splitting on mismatch; a structural un-copy is cheaper when the originating duplicator is still linked. Lattice details are disp proposals.

sources.title: Fractional Types: Expressive and Safe Space Management for Ancilla Bits (Chen, Choudhury, Carette, Sabry 2020)
sources.quote: garbage collection (GC) process specialized to reclaim, and only reclaim, storage containing the value false
sources.mechanism: Π is extended with a type 1/v and two combinators witnessing A × 1/A = 1 ([p.5-6](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.07020#page=6)): η_v : 1 ↔ τ × 1/v creates v with its reclaimer; ε_v : τ × 1/v ↔ 1 checks the incoming value equals v and returns unit, otherwise the interpreter 'throws an exception' (p.6). The reclaimer is first-class and 'can be manipulated, decomposed into smaller processes' (p.1). A richer type system with pointed types lifts programs so the runtime check can be removed (p.2).
sources.relevance: The most direct formal version of 'erasure is free relative to what the system knows'. For disp, anti-trees (co-L, co-S, co-F) could play 1/v, annihilating their tree layer by layer and refunding fuel; a mismatch is the exception case. Treating a duplicator's second output as the reclaimer for the first is a disp idea.

sources.title: Quantum Information Effects (Heunen & Kaarsgaard 2022)
sources.quote: Interestingly, though the languages and semantics are different, cloning is defined precisely as for classical information effects
sources.mechanism: Starts from Π and its unitary extension UΠ, then adds two arrow effects: allocation of ancillae on a hidden heap and hiding (discard). Derived combinators include clone (by induction on the type, p.11), merge : b + b ↣ b, defined by hiding the tag via a + a ≅ a × (1+1) (p.14), and measure = clone >>> fst, which classically 'is a complicated way of doing absolutely nothing' ([p.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12144#page=14)). Categorically the constructions turn bijections into functions with chosen garbage, reformulating Toffoli's theorem (p.2).
sources.relevance: Names the information effects in a tree-calculus step under disp's reading: S rule as clone, K as discard, triage as merge (forgetting a trit) plus discard of two arms. So a priced core needs one allocation effect (fuel) and one hiding effect (heat). On a quantum substrate copy-then-discard is a measurement.

sources.title: FP²: Fully in-Place Functional Programming (Lorenzen, Leijen, Swierstra 2023, MSR-TR-2023-19)
sources.quote: This "diamond" resource type ⋄k represents a specific heap cell of size k
sources.mechanism: Owned variables are used exactly once; borrowed parameters (^f) are read-only. A destructive match on a k-field constructor yields its fields plus a reuse credit ⋄k (that exact heap cell); building a k-field constructor consumes a ⋄k. Unlike space credits, 'a reuse credit can not be split or merged with other credits' (p.3). An application f(e) is 'a borrowed use of f' ([p.5](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/fip-tr-v2.pdf#page=5)). Underneath, Perceus emits 'precise reference counting instructions' with reuse analysis for guaranteed in-place updates ([Perceus p.1](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/perceus-tr-v4.pdf#page=1)).
sources.relevance: Could turn disp's global ledger into a local conservation law: a rewrite outputs exactly the cells it consumed, matched by size (for tree calculus, stem cells and fork cells differ in arity); surplus becomes local blanks (fuel), shortfall draws from neighbours. Borrowing gives the rule that applying a program never consumes it. These are disp proposals.

key_ideas: Three-line price list. Copying onto a blank costs no heat but uses up the blank (fuel); un-copying against a copy known to be identical costs no heat and returns the blank; erasing information that exists nowhere else costs kT ln 2 per bit (heat). Sources: [Bennett 2003](https://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0210005#page=2), [Landauer 1961](https://sites.pitt.edu/~jdnorton/lectures/Rotman_Summer_School_2013/thermo_computing_docs/Landauer_1961.pdf#page=4). In tree calculus (disp's own reading), only K and triage are many-to-one, so they are the only places heat can arise.

'Known identical' must be witnessed locally, two ways. Structural: the duplicator or fan that made both copies still links them, and un-copy is an annihilation (δδ in [Lafont](https://dcreager.net/pdf/Lafont1997.pdf#page=14), equal-index fans in [Baillot et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0704.2448#page=1)). By comparison: an agent zipping two trees layer by layer, like Rfun's ⌊·⌋ ([Kaarsgaard & Rennela](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.09929#page=3)), rolling back on mismatch. Prefer structural, fall back to comparison.

Make dup/eq one self-inverse agent. Rfun's ⌊<x>⌋ = <x,x>, ⌊<x,x>⌋ = <x>, ⌊<x,y>⌋ = <x,y> for x ≠ y is total and its own inverse ([Kaarsgaard & Rennela](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.09929#page=3)); it would replace iso.rs's partial Dup and its separate inverse.

History as particles left in place, not a log. Bennett's history is redundant with the machine and 'may be exploited to erase it reversibly' by running backward, at about twice the steps ([Bennett 1973](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall06/cos576/papers/bennett73.html#Introduction)). disp could leave K/triage residue where it was dropped instead of in records keyed by ids. If history space must be bounded, Bennett's pebbling uses the least extra space among pebble strategies ([Li & Vitányi](https://arxiv.org/pdf/quant-ph/9703022#page=1)).

Triage is the irreversible core. Weakening and contraction (K and S) can be made reversible by re-using circuits, but 'this fails for the additives' ([Abramsky p.25](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=25)). In effect terms (disp's mapping), triage = merge (forget which of three cases, a trit) + discard of two arms ([Heunen & Kaarsgaard p.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12144#page=14)). Arms copied by the S rule can often be dropped by un-copy; only the trit is truly new loss: keep it as a history particle or pay heat for log2(3) bits.

Copying is 'add onto zero'. Janus's '+= adds the expression into the variable. -= subtracts it out', with the variable barred from its own expression ([Lutz & Derby](https://www.tetsuo.jp/ref/janus.pdf#page=2)). Copy is += onto a blank and un-copy is -= of a known-equal value; Bennett's XOR register form is the bitwise case ([Bennett 2003](https://arxiv.org/pdf/physics/0210005#page=2)). A generalized duplicator accumulating onto a target covers both; a read in a linear net is copy-then-un-copy, net fuel 0.

Anti-trees as first-class knowledge. A reclaimer 1/v annihilates exactly v, is first-class, and can be decomposed into smaller reclaimers ([fractional types](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.07020#page=1)). On the lattice, co-L/co-S/co-F agents could cancel a tree layer by layer and refund fuel, so an erasure is free exactly when a matching anti-tree is in reach.

Conserve cells so fuel is local. Reuse credits ⋄k, which cannot be split or merged ([FP²](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/fip-tr-v2.pdf#page=3)), make each rewrite recycle consumed cells into built cells of the same size. Leftovers become local blanks, shortfalls draw from neighbours: a particle-number conservation law that removes the global ledger. Applying code is a borrowed use ([p.5](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/fip-tr-v2.pdf#page=5)).

Three regimes for re-use versus copy. (1) Re-use the circuit and tag tokens (geometry of interaction): reversible, no garbage, but recomputation and growing token words ([Abramsky](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.7154#page=11), [Danos & Regnier](https://www.pure.ed.ac.uk/ws/files/16874549/Reversible_irreversible_and_optimal_machines.pdf#page=4)). (2) Share and copy lazily (optimal reduction): local and oracle-free for EAL/LAL-typable terms; its non-elementary cost comes from apparently unavoidable duplication work, not bookkeeping ([Asperti p.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.04240#page=5)). (3) Copy eagerly with duplicators for parallel demand. Rule of thumb: borrow for big code with few uses, share by default, copy where parallelism pays for the fuel.

Copy budgets on duplicators. BLL's !_n A keeps weakening, dereliction, contraction and promotion valid with bounds 0, 1, + and · ([Girard LLL p.2](https://girard.perso.math.cnrs.fr/LLL.pdf#page=2)). A duplicator could carry its remaining copy allowance, a static local fuel bound. Levels (stratification) are what let fan labels work without the oracle ([Baillot et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0704.2448#page=1)).

Quantum constraint. A linear 'deleter' of an unknown state is only a swap into the ancilla ([Pati & Braunstein](https://arxiv.org/pdf/quant-ph/9911090#page=1)), so copying and un-copying are defined only in a fixed basis. A duplicator on a superposition entangles, and copy-then-discard is a measurement ([Heunen & Kaarsgaard p.14](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.12144#page=14)). Tree data stays classical; the repo's superposition agent under a duplicator is entangling fanout.

Annihilations need a residue to be reversible. γγ and δδ annihilation are 'disconnected' rules ([Salikhmetov p.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.07275#page=4)): the wires left behind do not record where the pair was. Making them reversible needs a residue (the repo's Seam) or connected rules, e.g. a small bond particle left on the joined wire, erasable later for heat or kept as history.

field: Stochastic thermodynamics of computation: how much heat a step has to cost given what the machine knows, and how much extra heat locality adds

sources.title: Thermodynamics of information (Parrondo, Horowitz, Sagawa, Nature Physics 2015); equations taken from Parrondo's 2023 chapter 'Thermodynamics of Information', arXiv 2306.12447
sources.quote: does it depend, for example, on what we know about the system?
sources.mechanism: The 2015 page only gives the abstract, which is where the quote MATCHes. The equations come from Parrondo 2023 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12447#page=6, MATCH: 'is a thermodynamic resource and can be used to define efficiencies for information and hybrid engines'). Nonequilibrium free energy is F(p) = <E>_p - kT S(p). Second law: W >= dF. A measurement into memory M raises X's free energy, averaged over outcomes, by exactly kT I(X;M) (Eq. 27, p.6). Feedback obeys W_fb >= dF - kT I(X;M) (Eq. 29, p.6). Counting the measurement itself, W_meas >= dF_Y + kT I(X;M) (Eq. 41, p.9), and W_meas + W_fb + W_reset >= 0 over the whole cycle (Eq. 42). So 'entropy relative to what the system knows' is the conditional entropy S(X|M).
sources.relevance: Supports pricing a lattice configuration by free energy, with entropy taken conditional on what the lattice still holds, so that a correlated record or copy counts as stored free energy (kT I) rather than waste. That only information nothing else carries must become heat is the global-optimum accounting. Local rules pay more on top of it (see Boyd-Mandal-Crutchfield 2018 and Ouldridge-Wolpert 2023).

sources.title: Thermodynamic and logical reversibilities revisited
sources.quote: any logically irreversible computation can be performed in a thermodynamically reversible manner in the quasi-static limit
sources.mechanism: Generalized Landauer bound (Eq. 61, p.18): heat emitted -Q >= kT(-dH - dS_in), where H is the entropy of the logical state and S_in the entropy inside each logical cell. Quasi-static erasure of a fair bit (remove the wall, compress) emits kT ln2, has zero entropy production, and running it in reverse restores the ensemble distribution, though not the individual bit (pp.13-14). For a biased bit with p != 1/2, first move the wall quasi-statically to volume ratio p:(1-p), then remove it; this also meets the generalized bound (p.24).
